name: Rugemont Castle
text: Your train passes near the site of Rugemont Castle, on the train's {side}, the earthworks of an early medieval ringwork, thought to have been a timber castle of the Wahull family and later of the de Greys. Much of it was destroyed when the Round House was built on the site in the 19th century.

name: Husborne Crawley railway station
text: Your train passes the site of Husborne Crawley station, which served the village from 1905 to 1941. Like the other halts on the line, it closed in 1917 to save money in the war, and reopened in 1919.

name: Woburn Sands
text: Your train passes Woburn Sands, on the train's {side}, a town that straddles the border between Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire, so that two police forces, Bedfordshire and Thames Valley, look after it. Its name comes from nearby Woburn and the sandy soil of the Greensand Ridge.

name: Cow Roast
text: Your train passes Cow Roast, on the train's {side}, a hamlet on the site of a Romano-British settlement near Akeman Street. Its name is almost certainly a corruption of "Cow Rest", from the pens where cattle rested on a drovers' route to London.

name: Berkhamsted Castle
text: Your train passes Berkhamsted Castle, on the train's {side}, a Norman motte-and-bailey castle taken in 1216 by Prince Louis of France after a siege of 20 days. The 1833 act for the London and Birmingham Railway protected it, so the line was built across the valley floor instead.

name: Frogmore Paper Mill
text: Your train passes near Frogmore Paper Mill, on the train's {side}, the oldest mechanical paper mill in the world, on an island in the River Gade. The world's first mechanised paper machine was installed here in 1803, paid for by the Fourdrinier brothers, whose costs had bankrupted them by 1810.

name: Nash Mill
text: Your train passes near the site of Nash Mill, on the train's {side}, a paper mill bought by John Dickinson in 1811 and soon known for the tough, thin paper of Bagster's Pocket Reference Bible. It made paper until 2006; Nash House, the Dickinsons' home, still stands.

name: Watford Tunnels
text: Your train goes through one of the Watford Tunnels. The first, a little more than a mile long, was built in 1837 to Robert Stephenson's design, after the Earl of Clarendon refused to let the line cross his Cassiobury estate; the second was added just to the east when the line was widened in the 1870s.

name: Watford railway station (1837–1858)
text: Your train passes near Watford's first station, on the train's {side}, a small single-storey red-brick building on St Albans Road, opened by the London and Birmingham Railway in 1837 and replaced by Watford Junction in 1858. Its ticket office still stands and is listed Grade II.

name: Stanborough Park Church
text: Your train passes near Stanborough Park, on the train's {side}, once home to the British headquarters of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, with the Stanborough Press, the Granose Foods factory and a sanatorium. The church in its grounds was dedicated in 1928.

name: Building Research Establishment
text: Your train passes near the Building Research Establishment, on the train's {side}, where secret work was done during the Second World War on the bouncing bomb for the Dambusters Raid of 1943. A small-scale model of the Möhne Dam, used for testing, is still there.

name: Spielplatz
text: Your train passes near Spielplatz, on the train's {side}, the longest-running naturist resort in the United Kingdom, its name German for "playground". Charles and Dorothy Macaskie founded it in 1929, moving from London into a tent in woodland they had bought.

name: Moor Mill Quarry, West
text: Your train passes near Moor Mill Quarry, on the train's {side}, a geological Site of Special Scientific Interest whose layers show the ice of the Anglian glaciation, about 450,000 years ago, turning the Thames from its old, more northerly course. Natural England calls it the only site that shows this diversion.

name: Sopwell Priory
text: Your train passes near the ruins of Sopwell Priory, on the train's {side}, a Benedictine nunnery founded around 1140 as a dependency of St Albans Abbey. After the Dissolution, Sir Richard Lee pulled it down and built a house on the site; the ruins stand on Cottonmill Lane.

name: The Royal Masonic School for Girls
text: Your train passes near the Royal Masonic School for Girls, on the train's {side}, founded in 1788 to care for the daughters of poor Freemasons. It opened with 15 pupils in Somers Town, London, in 1789 and moved here in 1934.

name: St Martin's Church, Stamford
text: Your train passes St Martin's Church, on the train's {side}, rebuilt in the Perpendicular style between 1482 and 1485 on the site of a church first built in the 12th century. Its Cecil Chapel holds the tombs of the Cecil family, among them William Cecil, the first Lord Burghley.

name: Must Farm
text: Your train passes near Must Farm, on the train's {side}, where five Bronze Age houses, built on stilts above a river around 950 BC, were found remarkably well preserved: a sudden fire brought them down into the river's silt. It has been called "Britain's Pompeii".

name: Nene Viaduct
text: Your train crosses the River Nene on the Nene Viaduct, or on the bridge built beside it in 1924. The viaduct, designed by William and Joseph Cubitt for the Great Northern Railway, was finished in 1850 as one of the last parts of the line between London and Werrington, and is listed Grade II*.

name: Hinchingbrooke House
text: Your train passes near Hinchingbrooke House, on the train's {side}, built around an 11th-century nunnery and given to the Cromwell family after the Reformation. It later became the home of the Earls of Sandwich, among them the fourth Earl, said to have invented the sandwich, and is now part of Hinchingbrooke School.

name: Little Barford Power Station
text: Your train passes Little Barford Power Station, on the train's {side}, a gas-fired station beside the River Great Ouse that can supply more than half a million homes. It stands on the site of two coal-fired power stations, opened in 1939 and 1959.

name: The Lodge RSPB reserve
text: Your train passes near The Lodge, on the train's {side}, the headquarters of the RSPB, in a nature reserve on the Greensand Ridge. Since 2005 work has gone on to bring back the heathland that covered the area before it was ploughed or planted with conifers in the 19th century.

name: Etonbury Castle
text: Your train passes near the site of Etonbury Castle, on the train's {side}, an ancient timber castle with a ringwork and one or two baileys, said to have been built by the Danes. A railway built through it destroyed the site, and only cropmarks and some earthworks remain.

name: Arlesey Old Moat and Glebe Meadows
text: Your train passes Arlesey Old Moat and Glebe Meadows, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve in a long, narrow strip between the River Hiz and the railway. Frogs, toads and newts spawn in the moat, and the meadows were bought for the public by a local group, Arlesey Conservation for Nature.

name: Six Hills
text: Your train passes near the Six Hills, on the train's {side}, six large mounds beside the old Great North Road, the largest surviving group of Roman barrows in England. Local legend says the Devil made them, throwing clods of earth at travellers and missing six times.

name: Wilbury Hill Camp
text: Your train passes near Wilbury Hill Camp, on the train's {side}, a late Bronze Age hill fort from about 700 BC, given stronger banks around 400 BC. Many Roman coins were found when its northern corner was quarried for railway ballast in the mid-19th century.

name: Spirella Building
text: Your train passes the Spirella Building, on the train's {side}, a corset factory begun in 1912 for the British arm of the American Spirella Company, designed by Cecil Hignett in the Arts and Crafts style. The factory closed in 1989.

name: Ivel Springs
text: Your train passes near Ivel Springs, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve whose springs are the source of the River Ivel. It was a rubbish dump until the 1950s, and part of its meadow is the site of a farming settlement protected as a scheduled monument.

name: Therfield Heath
text: Your train passes near Therfield Heath, on the train's {side}, a chalk common where sheep still graze, with a long barrow thought to be Neolithic and the largest known cemetery of round barrows in Hertfordshire. King James I is said to have liked to hunt here.

name: Royston Cave
text: Your train passes near Royston Cave, on the train's {side}, an ancient man-made cave under the town centre, rediscovered in 1742 where Ermine Street crosses the Icknield Way. Nobody knows who made it or why; a link with the Knights Templar is popular but unlikely.

name: L-Moor, Shepreth
text: Your train passes L-Moor, on the train's {side}, a stretch of unploughed calcareous grassland that is a Site of Special Scientific Interest, with horseshoe vetch and felwort in its drier parts and devil's-bit scabious where it is wetter.

name: Shepreth
text: Your train passes Shepreth, on the train's {side}, a village listed in the Domesday Book as Esceprid. Its name means "sheep stream": sheep were washed here on their way to Cambridge.

name: Royal Papworth Hospital
text: Your train passes Royal Papworth Hospital, on the train's {side}, the UK's biggest heart and lung transplant centre, which moved here from Papworth Everard in 2019. At its old home, in August 1979, Terence English carried out the first successful heart transplant in the UK.

name: Cambridge University Botanic Garden
text: Your train passes near the Cambridge University Botanic Garden, on the train's {side}, created in 1831 by Professor John Stevens Henslow, Charles Darwin's mentor, and opened to the public in 1846. On July 25th 2019 it recorded 38.7°C, the second-highest temperature measured in the UK.

name: Nine Wells
text: Your train passes near Nine Wells, on the train's {side}, a small wood where springs at the foot of a chalk hill feed Hobson's Conduit, built between 1610 and 1614 to bring fresh water into Cambridge. The water comes out at a steady 10.2°C.

name: Duxford Chapel
text: Your train passes Duxford Chapel, on the train's {side}, all that survives of the Hospital of St John, mostly built around 1337 of flint rubble with limestone doorways and windows. Despite its name, it stands between Duxford and Whittlesford.

name: Wellcome Sanger Institute
text: Your train passes near the Wellcome Sanger Institute, on the train's {side}, a genetics research centre founded in 1992 and named after the double Nobel laureate Frederick Sanger. It made the largest single contribution to the finished sequence of the human genome.

name: St Mary the Virgin Church, Wendens Ambo
text: Your train passes near St Mary the Virgin, Wendens Ambo, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed church whose oldest part, the 11th-century tower, carries a Hertfordshire spike. The village's name comes from the joining of Wenden Magna and Wenden Parva in 1662.

name: Leper Stone
text: Your train passes the Leper Stone, on the train's {side}, a large sarsen stone probably named after a medieval hospital for lepers nearby. Passers-by may have left alms for the patients in a small hollow on its top.

name: Elsenham
text: Your train passes Elsenham, on the train's {side}, best known for Elsenham Jam, made on Sir Walter Gilbey's estate and sold as "the most expensive jam in the world". Golden Miller, who won the Cheltenham Gold Cup five times between 1932 and 1936, is buried at Elsenham Stud.

name: Stansted Mountfitchet Castle
text: Your train passes Mountfitchet Castle, on the train's {side}, a Norman ringwork and bailey built on high ground by the Montfitchet family after the Conquest. Finds suggest the site was used in the Iron Age and by Romans, Saxons and Vikings; today it is a living-history museum.
